Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: The diagram shows an isosceles right-angled triangle $ABC$. $AE = DE = 1$ unit and $\angle ACD = 30^\circ$. a (i) Calculate the exact length of $CE$.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: Use $\triangle ADE$ to find $AD$, then use the sine rule in $\triangle ADC$ to find $AC$ and hence $CE=AC-AE$.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: $AE=DE=1,\ \triangle ADE\text{ is right-angled isosceles at }E\Rightarrow AD^2=1^2+1^2=2\Rightarrow AD=\sqrt2;\ \text{in }\triangle ADC,\ AD/\sin30^\circ = AC/\sin105^\circ\Rightarrow AC=AD\cdot\dfrac{\sin105^\circ}{\sin30^\circ}=\sqrt2\cdot\dfrac{\sin(60^\circ+45^\circ)}{1/2}=\sqrt2\cdot\dfrac{\frac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{4}}{1/2}=\sqrt2\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{2}=\sqrt3+1;\ CE=AC-AE=(\sqrt3+1)-1=\sqrt3.$

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: Divide the equation by $\cos x\cos y$ and solve the resulting linear equation in $\tan y$.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: $\dfrac{\sin x\cos y}{\cos x\cos y}+3\dfrac{\cos x\sin y}{\cos x\cos y}=2\dfrac{\sin x\sin y}{\cos x\cos y}-4\dfrac{\cos x\cos y}{\cos x\cos y}\Rightarrow\tan x+3\tan y=2\tan x\tan y-4;$ letting $\tan x=t,\ \tan y=u$ gives $t+3u=2tu-4\Rightarrow3u-2tu=-4-t\Rightarrow u(3-2t)=-(4+t)\Rightarrow u=\dfrac{t+4}{2t-3};$ hence $\tan y=\dfrac{\tan x+4}{2\tan x-3}.$

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Without attempting to solve them, state how many solutions the equation $\sin\theta=-\cos\theta$ has in the interval $0^\circ\le\theta\le360^\circ$.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: $\sin\theta=-\cos\theta\Rightarrow\tan\theta=-1$. The reference angle is $45^\circ$ and $\tan\theta<0$ in quadrants II and IV, so $\theta=135^\circ,315^\circ$. Hence there are $\boxed{2\text{ solutions}}$.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Without attempting to solve them, state how many solutions the equation $2\sin\theta+3\cos\theta+6=0$ has in the interval $0^\circ\le\theta\le360^\circ$.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: Use the maximum possible value of $2\sin\theta+3\cos\theta$ as $R\sin(\theta+\alpha)$ with $R=\sqrt{2^2+3^2}$.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: The expression $2\sin\theta+3\cos\theta$ has range $[-\sqrt{13},\sqrt{13}]$ with $\sqrt{13}\approx3.6$, so $2\sin\theta+3\cos\theta+6\ge-3.6+6>0$ for all $\theta$, hence it can never be $0$ and there are $\boxed{0\text{ solutions}}$.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Without attempting to solve them, state how many solutions the equation $\tan\theta+\dfrac1{\tan\theta}=0$ has in the interval $0^\circ\le\theta\le360^\circ$.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: Multiply both sides by $\tan\theta$ (excluding $\tan\theta=0$) and inspect the resulting quadratic.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: $\tan\theta+\dfrac1{\tan\theta}=0\Rightarrow\tan^2\theta+1=0$, but $\tan^2\theta+1>0$ for all real $\theta$, so the equation has $\boxed{0\text{ solutions}}$.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: Group terms and factorise by grouping.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Solve the equation $4\sin\theta\cos\theta-\cos^2\theta+4\sin\theta-\cos\theta=0$ in the interval $0^\circ\le\theta\le360^\circ$.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: Factorise by grouping to get a product of two factors then solve each.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: $4\sin\theta\cos\theta-\cos^2\theta+4\sin\theta-\cos\theta=4\sin\theta(\cos\theta+1)-\cos\theta(\cos\theta+1)=(\cos\theta+1)(4\sin\theta-\cos\theta)=0$. So $\cos\theta+1=0$ or $4\sin\theta-\cos\theta=0$. First gives $\cos\theta=-1\Rightarrow\theta=180^\circ$. Second gives $4\sin\theta=\cos\theta\Rightarrow\tan\theta=\tfrac14$ with reference angle $\tan^{-1}(\tfrac14)\approx14.0^\circ$, so $\theta\approx14.0^\circ,194.0^\circ$. Thus $\theta\approx14.0^\circ,180^\circ,194.0^\circ$.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Express $4\cos3\theta-\sin(90^\circ-3\theta)$ as a single trigonometric function.
Hence solve $4\cos3\theta-\sin(90^\circ-3\theta)=2$ in the interval $0^\circ\le\theta\le360^\circ$, giving answers to $3$ significant figures.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: Use part (a) to write the equation as $3\cos3\theta=2$, then solve $\cos3\theta=\tfrac23$ for $3\theta$ between $0^\circ$ and $1080^\circ$.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: From (a), $3\cos3\theta=2\Rightarrow\cos3\theta=\tfrac23$. Let $\alpha=\cos^{-1}(\tfrac23)\approx48.2^\circ$. Then $3\theta=\alpha,360^\circ-\alpha,360^\circ+\alpha,720^\circ-\alpha,720^\circ+\alpha,1080^\circ-\alpha\approx48.2^\circ,311.8^\circ,408.2^\circ,671.8^\circ,768.2^\circ,1031.8^\circ$. Dividing by $3$ gives $\theta\approx16.1^\circ,103.9^\circ,136.1^\circ,223.9^\circ,256.1^\circ,343.9^\circ$ (all to $3$ s.f.).

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Hence find the values of $\theta$, to one decimal place, in the interval $0^\circ\le\theta\le360^\circ$ for which $2\sin2\theta=\cos2\theta$.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: Use $\tan2\theta=0.5$ so $2\theta$ lies in quadrants I and III between $0^\circ$ and $720^\circ$.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: From (a) $\tan2\theta=0.5$. Reference angle is $\alpha=\tan^{-1}(0.5)\approx26.6^\circ$. For $0^\circ\le2\theta\le720^\circ$, $2\theta=\alpha,180^\circ+\alpha,360^\circ+\alpha,540^\circ+\alpha\approx26.6^\circ,206.6^\circ,386.6^\circ,566.6^\circ$. Hence $\theta\approx13.3^\circ,103.3^\circ,193.3^\circ,283.3^\circ$ (to $1$ d.p.).

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Find all the values of $\theta$ in the interval $0^\circ\le\theta\le360^\circ$ for which $\cos(\theta+75^\circ)=0.5$.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: Set $\phi=\theta+75^\circ$, solve $\cos\phi=0.5$, then subtract $75^\circ$ and adjust into $[0^\circ,360^\circ]$.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: $\cos(\theta+75^\circ)=0.5\Rightarrow\cos\phi=0.5$ with $\phi=\theta+75^\circ$. Thus $\phi=60^\circ,300^\circ$ (mod $360^\circ$). Hence $\theta=-15^\circ,225^\circ$; adding $360^\circ$ to the negative value gives $\theta=225^\circ,345^\circ$. Therefore $\theta=225^\circ,345^\circ$.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Find all the values of $\theta$ in the interval $0^\circ\le\theta\le360^\circ$ for which $\sin2\theta=0.7$, giving answers to one decimal place.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: Solve for $2\theta$ in $[0^\circ,720^\circ]$ using $\alpha=\sin^{-1}(0.7)$ and the sine symmetry.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Find the values of $x$ in the interval $0^\circ\le x\le270^\circ$ which satisfy $\dfrac{\cos2x+0.5}{1-\cos2x}=2$.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: Set $c=\cos2x$, solve the linear equation in $c$, then solve $\cos2x=\tfrac12$ in $[0^\circ,540^\circ]$.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Find, in degrees, the values of $\theta$ in the interval $0^\circ\le\theta\le360^\circ$ for which $2\cos^2\theta-\cos\theta-1=\sin^2\theta$, giving answers to $1$ decimal place where appropriate.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: Use $\sin^2\theta=1-\cos^2\theta$ to form a quadratic in $\cos\theta$, solve, then convert to angles.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: Let $c=\cos\theta$. Then $2c^2-c-1=1-c^2\Rightarrow3c^2-c-2=0\Rightarrow(3c+2)(c-1)=0$, so $c=1$ or $c=-\tfrac23$. Thus $\cos\theta=1\Rightarrow\theta=0^\circ,360^\circ$, and $\cos\theta=-\tfrac23\Rightarrow\theta\approx131.8^\circ,228.2^\circ$. Hence $\theta\approx0^\circ,131.8^\circ,228.2^\circ,360^\circ$.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: A teacher asks a student to solve $2\sin3x=1$ for $-360^\circ\le x\le360^\circ$; the student writes $\sin3x=\tfrac12,\ 3x=30^\circ,\ x=10^\circ,\ \text{additional solution at }180^\circ-10^\circ=170^\circ$. Identify two mistakes.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: Compare the correct sine-solving procedure with what the student did.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: First, the student found only one value $3x=30^\circ$ instead of all values of $3x$ with $\sin3x=\tfrac12$ in the interval $-1080^\circ\le3x\le1080^\circ$. Second, the symmetry $180^\circ-\alpha$ must be applied to $3x$, not to $x$, so subtracting $10^\circ$ from $180^\circ$ to get another $x$ is incorrect and also misses many further solutions.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Solve the equation $2\sin3x=1$ in the interval $-360^\circ\le x\le360^\circ$.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: Set $y=3x$, solve $\sin y=\tfrac12$ for $-1080^\circ\le y\le1080^\circ$, then divide by $3$.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: $2\sin3x=1\Rightarrow\sin3x=\tfrac12$. Let $y=3x$. Then $\sin y=\tfrac12$ so $y=30^\circ+360^\circ k$ or $y=150^\circ+360^\circ k$. For $-1080^\circ\le y\le1080^\circ$ this gives $y=-1050^\circ,-690^\circ,-330^\circ,30^\circ,390^\circ,750^\circ,-930^\circ,-570^\circ,-210^\circ,150^\circ,510^\circ,870^\circ$. Dividing by $3$ yields $x=-350^\circ,-230^\circ,-110^\circ,10^\circ,130^\circ,250^\circ,-310^\circ,-190^\circ,-70^\circ,50^\circ,170^\circ,290^\circ$. Restricting to $-360^\circ\le x\le360^\circ$, the solutions are $x=-350^\circ,-310^\circ,-230^\circ,-190^\circ,-110^\circ,-70^\circ,10^\circ,50^\circ,130^\circ,170^\circ,250^\circ,290^\circ$.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Sketch the graphs of $y=3\sin x$ and $y=2\cos x$ on the same set of axes ($0^\circ\le x\le360^\circ$).
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: Mark key points using amplitudes $3$ and $2$ and the usual $90^\circ$ step for sine and cosine.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: $y=3\sin x$ is a sine wave with amplitude $3$ passing through $(0,0)$, $(90^\circ,3)$, $(180^\circ,0)$, $(270^\circ,-3)$, $(360^\circ,0)$. The graph $y=2\cos x$ has amplitude $2$ and passes through $(0^\circ,2)$, $(90^\circ,0)$, $(180^\circ,-2)$, $(270^\circ,0)$, $(360^\circ,2)$. Plot these key points and draw smooth periodic curves.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: From the graphs, write down how many solutions there are in the given range for the equation $3\sin x=2\cos x$.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: Observe how many intersection points the two curves have between $0^\circ$ and $360^\circ$.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: The graphs $y=3\sin x$ and $y=2\cos x$ intersect twice in $0^\circ\le x\le360^\circ$, once in quadrant I and once in quadrant III, so there are $\boxed{2}$ solutions.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Solve the equation $3\sin x=2\cos x$ algebraically, giving your answers in $0^\circ\le x\le360^\circ$ to one decimal place.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: Divide both sides by $\cos x$ to form a tangent equation and then use the CAST diagram.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: $3\sin x=2\cos x\Rightarrow\tan x=\dfrac{2}{3}$. The reference angle is $\alpha=\tan^{-1}\left(\tfrac23\right)\approx33.7^\circ$. Since $\tan x>0$, $x$ lies in quadrants I and III: $x\approx33.7^\circ$ or $x\approx180^\circ+33.7^\circ=213.7^\circ$. Thus $x\approx33.7^\circ,213.7^\circ$ (to $1$ d.p.).

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: The diagram shows triangle $ABC$ with $AB=11\text{ cm}$, $BC=6\text{ cm}$ and $AC=7\text{ cm}$. a Find the exact value of $\cos B$, giving your answer in simplest form.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: Use the cosine rule with side $AC$ opposite angle $B$.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: By the cosine rule, $AC^2=AB^2+BC^2-2(AB)(BC)\cos B\Rightarrow7^2=11^2+6^2-2\cdot11\cdot6\cos B\Rightarrow49=121+36-132\cos B\Rightarrow132\cos B=108\Rightarrow\cos B=\dfrac{108}{132}=\dfrac{9}{11}$.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Hence find the exact value of $\sin B$.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: Use $\sin^2B=1-\cos^2B$ and that $B$ is acute so $\sin B>0$.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: The diagram shows triangle $PQR$ with $PR=6\text{ cm}$, $QR=5\text{ cm}$ and angle $QPR=45^\circ$. a Show that $\sin Q=\dfrac{3\sqrt2}{5}$.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: Apply the sine rule with sides $PR$ and $QR$ opposite angles $Q$ and $P$.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: By the sine rule, $\dfrac{PR}{\sin Q}=\dfrac{QR}{\sin P}\Rightarrow\dfrac{6}{\sin Q}=\dfrac{5}{\sin45^\circ}=\dfrac{5}{\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}}=\dfrac{10}{\sqrt2}$. Hence $\sin Q=\dfrac{6\sqrt2}{10}=\dfrac{3\sqrt2}{5}$.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Given that $Q$ is obtuse, find the exact value of $\cos Q$.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: Use $\cos^2Q=1-\sin^2Q$ and choose the negative square root because $Q$ is obtuse.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: $\sin Q=\dfrac{3\sqrt2}{5}\Rightarrow\sin^2Q=\dfrac{18}{25}\Rightarrow\cos^2Q=1-\dfrac{18}{25}=\dfrac{7}{25}\Rightarrow\cos Q=-\dfrac{\sqrt7}{5}$ since $Q$ is obtuse and $\cos Q<0$.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Show that the equation $3\sin^2x-\cos^2x=2$ can be written as $4\sin^2x=3$.
Hence solve the equation $3\sin^2x-\cos^2x=2$ in the interval $-180^\circ\le x\le180^\circ$, giving your answers to one decimal place.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: Use $4\sin^2x=3$ to find $\sin x=\pm\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ and then list all such angles in the interval.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: From (a) $4\sin^2x=3\Rightarrow\sin^2x=\dfrac34\Rightarrow\sin x=\pm\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$. Thus $x=\pm60^\circ,\pm120^\circ$ in $[-180^\circ,180^\circ]$. To one decimal place, $x\approx-120.0^\circ,-60.0^\circ,60.0^\circ,120.0^\circ$.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Find all the solutions to the equation $3\cos^2x+1=4\sin x$ in the interval $-360^\circ\le x\le360^\circ$, giving your answers to $1$ decimal place.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: Rewrite $\cos^2x$ as $1-\sin^2x$, form a quadratic in $\sin x$, solve, then use the sine symmetry to list all angles in the interval.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: $3\cos^2x+1=4\sin x\Rightarrow3(1-\sin^2x)+1=4\sin x\Rightarrow4-3\sin^2x=4\sin x\Rightarrow3\sin^2x+4\sin x-4=0$. Let $s=\sin x$. Then $3s^2+4s-4=0\Rightarrow s=\dfrac{-4\pm\sqrt{16+48}}{6}=\dfrac{-4\pm8}{6}$, so $s=\dfrac23$ or $s=-2$ (rejected). Thus $\sin x=\dfrac23$. Reference angle $\alpha=\sin^{-1}\!\left(\tfrac23\right)\approx41.8^\circ$. General solutions are $x=\alpha+360k^\circ$ or $x=180^\circ-\alpha+360k^\circ$. For $-360^\circ\le x\le360^\circ$ this gives $x\approx41.8^\circ,138.2^\circ,-318.2^\circ,-221.8^\circ$. So $x\approx-318.2^\circ,-221.8^\circ,41.8^\circ,138.2^\circ$ (to $1$ d.p.).

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Solve the equation $\tan^2x-3\tan x+2=0$ in the interval $0^\circ\le x\le360^\circ$.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: Factor the quadratic in $\tan x$ and then solve $\tan x=1$ and $\tan x=2$ using the $180^\circ$ period.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: $\tan^2x-3\tan x+2=0\Rightarrow(\tan x-1)(\tan x-2)=0\Rightarrow\tan x=1\text{ or }\tan x=2$. For $\tan x=1$, $x=45^\circ,225^\circ$. For $\tan x=2$, reference angle $\beta=\tan^{-1}2\approx63.4^\circ$, so $x\approx63.4^\circ,243.4^\circ$. Hence $x\approx45.0^\circ,63.4^\circ,225.0^\circ,243.4^\circ$ (to $1$ d.p.).

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: $$\text{The graph shows }y=\sin(x+45^\circ)\text{ for }-360^\circ\le x\le 360^\circ.\ \text{Write down the coordinates of each point where the curve crosses the x-axis.}$$
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: $$\text{Set }y=0:\ \sin(x+45^\circ)=0\Rightarrow x+45^\circ=180^\circ n,\ n\in\mathbb{Z}.\ \text{List all }x\text{ in the given interval.}$$
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: $$\begin{aligned}\sin(x+45^\circ)=0&\Rightarrow x+45^\circ=180^\circ n\\x&=180^\circ n-45^\circ\\\text{Now choose integers }n\text{ so that }-360^\circ\le x\le360^\circ:\\n=-1&\Rightarrow x=-225^\circ\\n=0&\Rightarrow x=-45^\circ\\n=1&\Rightarrow x=135^\circ\\n=2&\Rightarrow x=315^\circ\\n=3&\Rightarrow x=495^\circ\ (\text{too large}),\ n=-2\Rightarrow x=-405^\circ\ (\text{too small})\\\Rightarrow\ \text{x-axis crossings: }&(-225^\circ,0),\ (-45^\circ,0),\ (135^\circ,0),\ (315^\circ,0)\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: $$\text{The graph shows }y=\sin(x+45^\circ)\text{ for }-360^\circ\le x\le 360^\circ.\ \text{Write down the coordinates of the point where the curve crosses the y-axis.}$$
$$\text{A pyramid has four triangular faces and a square base. All the edges of the pyramid are the same length }s\text{ cm. Show that the total surface area is }(\sqrt3+1)s^2\text{ cm}^2.$$
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: $$\text{If all edges are }s,\ \text{each triangular face has three sides }s\Rightarrow\text{equilateral. Find area of 4 faces + base.}$$
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: $$\begin{aligned}\text{Base: }&\text{square of side }s\Rightarrow A_{\text{base}}=s^2\\\text{Each triangular face: }&\text{two slant edges }=s\text{ and base edge }=s\\&\Rightarrow \text{each face is an equilateral triangle of side }s\\\text{Area of one equilateral triangle: }&A_{\triangle}=\frac{\sqrt3}{4}s^2\\\text{Four faces: }&A_{\text{faces}}=4\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{4}s^2=\sqrt3\,s^2\\\text{Total surface area: }&A_{\text{total}}=A_{\text{base}}+A_{\text{faces}}=s^2+\sqrt3\,s^2=(\sqrt3+1)s^2\ \text{cm}^2\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: $$\text{Find all solutions in }0^\circ\le x<360^\circ\text{ of }2\tan^2x-4=5\tan x,\ \text{giving each solution to 1 d.p.}$$
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: $$\text{Let }t=\tan x.\ \text{Solve the quadratic }2t^2-5t-4=0,\ \text{then convert each }t\text{ to angles in }[0^\circ,360^\circ).$$
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: $$\begin{aligned}2\tan^2x-4&=5\tan x\\\text{Let }t=\tan x\Rightarrow 2t^2-5t-4&=0\\t&=\frac{5\pm\sqrt{25+32}}{4}=\frac{5\pm\sqrt{57}}{4}\\\sqrt{57}&\approx7.5498\\t_1&=\frac{5+7.5498}{4}\approx3.1375,\quad t_2=\frac{5-7.5498}{4}\approx-0.6375\\\text{Now find angles: }&x=\arctan(t)+180^\circ k\\\arctan(3.1375)&\approx72.2^\circ\Rightarrow x\approx72.2^\circ,\ 252.2^\circ\\\arctan(-0.6375)&\approx-32.5^\circ\Rightarrow x\approx147.5^\circ,\ 327.5^\circ\\\Rightarrow\ \text{Solutions: }&x\approx72.2^\circ,\ 147.5^\circ,\ 252.2^\circ,\ 327.5^\circ\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: $$\text{Find all solutions in }0^\circ\le x<360^\circ\text{ of }5\sin^2x=6(1-\cos x),\ \text{giving each solution to 1 d.p.}$$
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: $$\text{Use }\sin^2x=1-\cos^2x.\ \text{Let }c=\cos x\text{ to get a quadratic, then convert back to angles.}$$
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: $$\begin{aligned}5\sin^2x&=6(1-\cos x)\\5(1-\cos^2x)&=6-6\cos x\\5-5\cos^2x&=6-6\cos x\\0&=1-6\cos x+5\cos^2x\\5c^2-6c+1&=0\quad(c=\cos x)\\c&=\frac{6\pm\sqrt{36-20}}{10}=\frac{6\pm4}{10}\\\Rightarrow c&=1\ \text{or}\ c=0.2\\\cos x=1&\Rightarrow x=0^\circ\ (\text{and }360^\circ\text{ excluded})\\\cos x=0.2&\Rightarrow x=\arccos(0.2)\approx78.5^\circ\ \text{or}\ 360^\circ-78.5^\circ\approx281.5^\circ\\\Rightarrow\ \text{Solutions: }&x\approx0.0^\circ,\ 78.5^\circ,\ 281.5^\circ\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: $$\text{Prove that }\cos^2x(\tan^2x+1)=1\text{ for all }x\text{ where }\cos x\text{ and }\tan x\text{ are defined.}$$
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: $$\text{Use }\tan x=\frac{\sin x}{\cos x}\text{ and }\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.\ \text{Simplify step by step.}$$

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: $$\text{Use your calculator to find the principal solution of }\tan x=-2$$
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: $$\text{From the sketch, the principal solution is the first solution in }0^\circ<x<180^\circ\ (\text{between }90^\circ\text{ and }180^\circ)$$
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: $$\begin{aligned}\tan x&=-2\\\text{Calculator gives }x&=\tan^{-1}(-2)\approx-63.4349^\circ\\\text{But on }0^\circ\le x\le180^\circ,\ \tan x<0\text{ occurs in quadrant II, so}\\x&=180^\circ-63.4349^\circ=116.5651^\circ\\\therefore\ \text{principal solution }x&\approx116.6^\circ\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: $$\text{Use the graph and your answer to (a) to solve }\tan x=-2\text{ for }0^\circ\le x\le360^\circ$$
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: $$\tan x\text{ has period }180^\circ,\ \text{so add }180^\circ\text{ to get the next solution}$$

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: $$\text{Use your calculator to find the principal solution of }\cos x=0.4$$
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: $$\text{For cosine, the principal solution is the angle in }0^\circ\le x\le180^\circ$$

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: $$\text{Use the graph and your answer to (a) to solve }\cos x=\pm0.4\text{ for }0^\circ\le x\le360^\circ$$

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: $$\begin{aligned}\sin\theta&=-1\\\text{On the unit circle, }\sin\theta=-1&\text{ at the bottom point}\\\therefore\ \theta&=270^\circ\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: $$\text{If }\sin\theta<0,\ \theta\text{ is in quadrants III and IV}$$

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: $$\begin{aligned}\sin x&=-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\\x&=-60^\circ+360^\circ k\ \text{ or }\ x=240^\circ+360^\circ k\\\text{List values in }[-180^\circ,540^\circ]:\\x&=-60^\circ\ (k=0),\ 300^\circ\ (k=1)\\x&=-120^\circ\ (240^\circ-360^\circ),\ 240^\circ\\\therefore\ x&=-120^\circ,\ -60^\circ,\ 240^\circ,\ 300^\circ\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: $$\sin x=-0.15,\ \text{negative in quadrants III and IV; use negative angles in this interval}$$
$$\cos x\text{ is even, so solutions are }\pm\cos^{-1}(-0.809)$$
$$\cos x=0.84\Rightarrow x=\pm\cos^{-1}(0.84)+360^\circ k,\ \text{then choose negative solutions}$$
$$x=\tan^{-1}(2.90)+180^\circ k,\ \text{then keep values in the interval}$$
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: $$\begin{aligned}\tan x&=2.90\\\beta&=\tan^{-1}(2.90)\approx70.0^\circ\\x&=\beta+180^\circ k\\\text{Check the interval }80^\circ\le x\le440^\circ:\\k=0:&\ x\approx70.0^\circ\ (\text{too small})\\k=1:&\ x\approx250.0^\circ\ (\text{ok})\\k=2:&\ x\approx430.0^\circ\ (\text{ok})\\\therefore\ x&\approx250^\circ,\ 430^\circ\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: $$\text{Dividing by }\cos x\text{ should give }\tan x=\frac{2}{3},\text{ not }\frac{3}{2}$$
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: $$\begin{aligned}2\cos x&=3\sin x\\\text{Divide by }\cos x:\ 2&=3\tan x\\\Rightarrow \tan x&=\frac{2}{3}\ (\text{correct})\\\text{Student A wrote }\tan x&=\frac{3}{2}\ (\text{inverted the fraction})\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: $$\text{For }2\cos x=3\sin x,\ \text{identify Student B's mistake and its effect}$$
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: $$\text{Student B squared, which loses sign information and can create extra solutions}$$
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: $$\begin{aligned}\text{Student B squares: }(2\cos x)^2&=(3\sin x)^2\\4\cos^2x&=9\sin^2x\\\text{But squaring makes }2\cos x&=\pm3\sin x\\\text{so it allows solutions where }\tan x&=-\frac23\ \text{as well}\\\text{Effect: it produces extra (incorrect) solutions that do not satisfy the original equation.}\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: $$\text{Sketch }y=2\sin x\text{ and }y=\cos x\text{ on the same axes for }0^\circ\le x\le360^\circ$$
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: $$\text{Use key points (intercepts/max/min) for each curve, then draw smooth sinusoidal curves}$$
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: $$\begin{aligned}\text{For }y=2\sin x:&\\x=0^\circ,180^\circ,360^\circ&:\ y=0\\x=90^\circ&:\ y=2\ (\text{maximum})\\x=270^\circ&:\ y=-2\ (\text{minimum})\\[4pt]\text{For }y=\cos x:&\\x=0^\circ&:\ y=1\ (\text{maximum})\\x=90^\circ,270^\circ&:\ y=0\\x=180^\circ&:\ y=-1\ (\text{minimum})\\\text{Plot these points and join with smooth curves on the same axes.}\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: $$\text{How many solutions are there for }2\sin x=\cos x\text{ in }0^\circ\le x\le360^\circ?$$
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: $$2\sin x=\cos x\Rightarrow\tan x=\frac12,\ \text{which has 2 solutions in one full turn}$$
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: $$\begin{aligned}2\sin x&=\cos x\\\tan x&=\frac{1}{2}\\\text{Since }\tan x\text{ has period }180^\circ,\ \text{there are two solutions in }[0^\circ,360^\circ].\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: $$\text{Find all values of }\theta\text{ (to 1 d.p.) in }0^\circ<\theta<360^\circ\text{ such that }\tan^2\theta=9$$
$$\text{Use your answer to (a) to explain why }2\sin^2x+5\cos^2x=1\text{ has no solution}$$
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: $$\begin{aligned}\text{From (a): }2\sin^2x+5\cos^2x=1&\iff 3\sin^2x=4\\\Rightarrow \sin^2x&=\frac43\\\text{But for any real }x,\ 0\le\sin^2x&\le1\\\frac43&>1\ \Rightarrow\ \text{impossible}\\\therefore\ \text{the equation has no real solution.}\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}4\cos^2\theta-5\sin\theta-5&=0\\4(1-s^2)-5s-5&=0\\4-4s^2-5s-5&=0\\-4s^2-5s-1&=0\\4s^2+5s+1&=0\\(4s+1)(s+1)&=0\\s&=-\frac14\ \text{or}\ s=-1\\\text{But in }0^\circ\le\theta\le180^\circ,\ \sin\theta&\ge0\\\Rightarrow s<0\text{ is impossible in this interval}\\\therefore\ \text{no solution in }[0^\circ,180^\circ]\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: $$\text{Find all solutions in }0^\circ\le x\le360^\circ\text{ to }8\sin^2x+6\cos x-9=0,\ \text{giving each solution to 1 d.p.}$$
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: $$\text{Write }\sin^2x=1-\cos^2x,\ \text{let }c=\cos x,\ \text{solve the quadratic, then convert back to angles.}$$
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: $$\begin{aligned}8\sin^2x+6\cos x-9&=0\\8(1-\cos^2x)+6\cos x-9&=0\\8-8\cos^2x+6\cos x-9&=0\\-8\cos^2x+6\cos x-1&=0\\8\cos^2x-6\cos x+1&=0\\\text{Let }c=\cos x:\quad 8c^2-6c+1&=0\\c&=\frac{6\pm\sqrt{36-32}}{16}=\frac{6\pm2}{16}\\c&=\frac12\ \text{or}\ \frac14\\[4pt]\cos x=\frac12&\Rightarrow x=60^\circ,\ 300^\circ\\[2pt]\cos x=\frac14&\Rightarrow x=\cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac14\right),\ 360^\circ-\cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac14\right)\\\cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac14\right)&\approx75.522^\circ\\x&\approx75.522^\circ,\ 284.478^\circ\\[4pt]\therefore\ x&=60.0^\circ,\ 75.5^\circ,\ 284.5^\circ,\ 300.0^\circ\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: $$\text{Find all solutions in }0^\circ\le x\le360^\circ\text{ to }\sin^2x+1=\frac{7}{2}\cos^2x,\ \text{giving each solution to 1 d.p.}$$
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: $$\begin{aligned}\sin^2x+1&=\frac{7}{2}\cos^2x\\(1-\cos^2x)+1&=\frac{7}{2}\cos^2x\\2-\cos^2x&=\frac{7}{2}\cos^2x\\2&=\left(\frac{7}{2}+1\right)\cos^2x=\frac{9}{2}\cos^2x\\\cos^2x&=\frac{4}{9}\\\Rightarrow \cos x&=\pm\frac{2}{3}\\[4pt]\cos x=\frac23:&\ x=\cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac23\right),\ 360^\circ-\cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac23\right)\\\cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac23\right)&\approx48.1897^\circ\\x&\approx48.1897^\circ,\ 311.8103^\circ\\[4pt]\cos x=-\frac23:&\ x=\cos^{-1}\!\left(-\frac23\right),\ 360^\circ-\cos^{-1}\!\left(-\frac23\right)\\\cos^{-1}\!\left(-\frac23\right)&\approx131.8103^\circ\\x&\approx131.8103^\circ,\ 228.1897^\circ\\[4pt]\therefore\ x&\approx48.2^\circ,\ 131.8^\circ,\ 228.2^\circ,\ 311.8^\circ\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: $$\text{Show that }2\cos^2x+\cos x-6=0\text{ has no solutions (in degrees).}$$
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: $$\text{Let }c=\cos x.\ \text{If the quadratic gives }|c|>1,\ \text{then no real }x\text{ exists.}$$
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: $$\begin{aligned}2\cos^2x+\cos x-6&=0\\\text{Let }c=\cos x:\quad 2c^2+c-6&=0\\c&=\frac{-1\pm\sqrt{1-4(2)(-6)}}{2\cdot2}=\frac{-1\pm\sqrt{49}}{4}\\c&=\frac{-1\pm7}{4}\\c&=\frac{6}{4}=1.5\ \text{ or }\ c=\frac{-8}{4}=-2\\\text{But }\cos x&\in[-1,1]\text{ for all real }x\\1.5\notin[-1,1],\ -2\notin[-1,1]&\Rightarrow \text{both are impossible}\\\therefore\ \text{the equation has no real solutions.}\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: $$\text{Show that } \cos^2x=2-\sin x \text{ can be written as } \sin^2x-\sin x+1=0$$
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: $$\cos^2x=1-\sin^2x,\ \text{then rearrange to a quadratic in }\sin x$$

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_title: Hence show cos^2x=2−sinx has no solutions
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: $$\text{Hence show that } \cos^2x=2-\sin x \text{ has no solutions.}$$
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: $$\text{Use the quadratic } \sin^2x-\sin x+1=0:\ \text{if its discriminant }<0,\text{ it has no real solutions.}$$
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: $$\begin{aligned}\sin^2x-\sin x+1&=0\\\text{Discriminant } \Delta&=b^2-4ac=(-1)^2-4(1)(1)\\&=1-4=-3<0\\\Rightarrow \sin x&\text{ cannot be real for any }x\\\therefore\ \text{there is no real }x\text{ satisfying }\cos^2x=2-\sin x.\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: $$\text{Given }\tan^2x-2\tan x-4=0,\ \text{show that }\tan x=p\pm\sqrt q\text{ and find }p,q$$

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: $$\begin{aligned}\tan^2x-2\tan x-4&=0\\\Rightarrow \tan x&=1+\sqrt5\ \text{or}\ 1-\sqrt5\\t_1&=1+\sqrt5\approx3.2361\\t_2&=1-\sqrt5\approx-1.2361\\[6pt]\textbf{For }t_1=3.2361:\\\alpha&=\tan^{-1}(3.2361)\approx72.828^\circ\\x&=\alpha+180^\circ k\\0^\circ\le x\le540^\circ\Rightarrow x&\approx72.828^\circ,\ 252.828^\circ,\ 432.828^\circ\\[6pt]\textbf{For }t_2=-1.2361:\\\beta&=\tan^{-1}(-1.2361)\approx-51.027^\circ\\\text{Equivalent angle in }[0^\circ,180^\circ]\text{ is }180^\circ-51.027^\circ&=128.973^\circ\\x&=128.973^\circ+180^\circ k\\0^\circ\le x\le540^\circ\Rightarrow x&\approx128.973^\circ,\ 308.973^\circ,\ 488.973^\circ\\[6pt]\therefore\ x&\approx72.8^\circ,\ 128.9^\circ,\ 252.8^\circ,\ 309.0^\circ,\ 432.8^\circ,\ 489.0^\circ\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Show that cos^2x = 2 − sinx can be written as sin^2x − sinx + 1 = 0.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: Start from cos^2x = 2 − sinx. Replace cos^2x using the identity cos^2x = 1 − sin^2x. Then 1 − sin^2x = 2 − sinx. Rearranging gives 0 = 2 − sinx − (1 − sin^2x) = 1 − sinx + sin^2x. Writing in standard quadratic form gives sin^2x − sinx + 1 = 0.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Hence show cos^2x = 2 − sinx has no real solutions.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: Use discriminant of quadratic in sinx.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: From Question 1, the equation becomes sin^2x − sinx + 1 = 0. For a quadratic ax^2+bx+c=0, real solutions exist only if the discriminant Δ=b^2−4ac≥0. Here a=1, b=−1, c=1. Δ=(−1)^2−4(1)(1)=1−4=−3<0. Since sinx must be real for real x, there are no real solutions.
Let u = sinx. Then u^2 − 3u + 2 = 0. Factorising gives (u−1)(u−2)=0, so u=1 or u=2. Since sinx cannot exceed 1, u=2 is rejected. Therefore sinx=1, which occurs at x=90°.
Factorising gives cosx(cosx−1)=0. Hence cosx=0 or cosx=1. cosx=0 occurs at x=90°,270°. cosx=1 occurs at x=0°,360°.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Show that sin^2x = 1 − cosx can be written as cos^2x + cosx − 1 = 0.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: Starting from sin^2x = 1 − cosx, substitute sin^2x = 1 − cos^2x. This gives 1 − cos^2x = 1 − cosx. Subtracting 1 from both sides yields −cos^2x = −cosx. Rearranging gives cos^2x + cosx − 1 = 0.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Show that cos^2x = 2 has no real solutions.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: For all real x, −1 ≤ cosx ≤ 1, so 0 ≤ cos^2x ≤ 1. Since 2 lies outside this range, the equation cos^2x = 2 has no real solutions.
Let u=sinx. Then u^2+2u−3=0. Factorising gives (u+3)(u−1)=0, so u=−3 or u=1. Since sinx∈[−1,1], u=−3 is rejected. Hence sinx=1, which gives x=90°.
cosx(cosx+2)=0. Hence cosx=0 or cosx=−2. cosx=−2 is impossible. Therefore cosx=0, giving x=90°,270°.
sinx = ±1/2. sinx=1/2 gives x=30°,150°. sinx=−1/2 gives x=210°,330°.
Let u=cosx. Then u^2+u−1=0. Using the quadratic formula, u = [−1±√(1+4)]/2 = (−1±√5)/2. Only (−1+√5)/2≈0.618 lies within [−1,1]. Hence cosx≈0.618. This gives x≈51.8° and x≈308.2°.
Let u=sinx. Then u=[1±√(1+4)]/2=(1±√5)/2. Only (1−√5)/2≈−0.618 is valid. Thus sinx≈−0.618, giving x≈218.2° and x≈321.8°.
Use cos^2x=1−sin^2x. Then 1−sin^2x=sinx ⇒ sin^2x+sinx−1=0. Solving gives sinx=(−1+√5)/2≈0.618. Hence x≈38.2°,141.8°.
Use sin^2x=1−cos^2x. Then 1−cos^2x=cosx ⇒ cos^2x+cosx−1=0. Solving gives cosx≈0.618, hence x≈51.8°,308.2°.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: Let u = sinx and solve the quadratic; then find all angles.
Let u = cosx; solve; then use cosine angles.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: Let u = sinx. Then u^2 + 4u + 3 = 0 ⇒ (u+1)(u+3)=0 ⇒ u = −1 or u = −3. Since sinx∈[−1,1], u = −3 is impossible. So sinx = −1 ⇒ x = 270°.
Let u = cosx. Then u^2 − 4u + 3 = 0 ⇒ (u−1)(u−3)=0 ⇒ u = 1 or u = 3. cosx cannot be 3, so cosx = 1 ⇒ x = 0°, 360°.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Show that sin^2x + 2sinx + 2 = 0 has no real solution.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: Check discriminant of quadratic in u=sinx.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: Let u = sinx. Then u^2 + 2u + 2 = 0. Discriminant Δ = 2^2 − 4·1·2 = 4 − 8 = −4 < 0, so u is not real. Since sinx must be real for real x, there is no real solution.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Show that cos^2x + 2cosx + 5 = 0 has no real solution.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: Let u = cosx. Then u^2 + 2u + 5 = 0 with Δ = 2^2 − 4·1·5 = 4 − 20 = −16 < 0. So no real u, hence no real x.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: Use 1−cos^2x = sin^2x, then quadratic in cosx.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: Start: 1 − cos^2x = cosx ⇒ bring all terms: cos^2x + cosx − 1 = 0. Let u = cosx. Then u = (−1 ± √5)/2. Only u = (−1+√5)/2 ≈ 0.618 is valid (the other is < −1). So cosx ≈ 0.618 ⇒ x ≈ 51.8°, 360°−51.8°=308.2°.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: Use 1−sin^2x = cos^2x; make quadratic in sinx.
Factorise in t=tanx, then solve angles using tan periodicity.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: Let t = tanx. Then t^2 + 6t + 5 = 0 ⇒ (t+1)(t+5)=0 ⇒ t = −1 or t = −5. If tanx = −1 ⇒ x = 135°, 315°. If tanx = −5 ⇒ principal angle is arctan(5)≈78.7°, so negative tan gives x≈180°−78.7°=101.3° and x≈360°−78.7°=281.3°.
Let u = cos(2x). Then u^2 − u − 2 = 0 ⇒ (u−2)(u+1)=0 ⇒ u=2 or u=−1. u=2 is impossible since |cos(2x)|≤1. So cos(2x)=−1 ⇒ 2x = 180° + 360°k ⇒ x = 90° + 180°k. In range: x = 90°, 270°.
Let u = sin(2x). Then u^2 + u − 2 = 0 ⇒ (u+2)(u−1)=0 ⇒ u=−2 or u=1. u=−2 impossible. So sin(2x)=1 ⇒ 2x=90°+360°k ⇒ x=45°+180°k. In range: x=45°,225°.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: tan(2x)=±2, then solve for x in range.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Show that sin^2x − sinx + 1 > 0 for all real x.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: Let u=sinx. Then u^2−u+1 = (u−1/2)^2 + 3/4. Since (u−1/2)^2 ≥ 0 for all real u, the expression is always ≥ 3/4 > 0. Hence it is strictly positive for all x.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Show that cos^2x + cosx + 1 > 0 for all real x.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: Let u=cosx. Then u^2+u+1 = (u+1/2)^2 + 3/4 ≥ 3/4 > 0. Therefore the expression is always positive for all x.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Solve sin^2x + sinx = 2 for real x.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: LHS = sin^2x + sinx. Since sinx∈[−1,1], the maximum of u^2+u occurs at u=1, giving 1^2+1=2. So equality is possible only when sinx=1. Hence x = 90° + 360°k.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Solve cos^2x − cosx = 2 for real x.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: Let u=cosx ∈ [−1,1]. Then u^2−u has maximum at an endpoint: u=−1 gives 1−(−1)=2, u=1 gives 0. So equality u^2−u=2 occurs only at u=−1. Thus cosx=−1 ⇒ x=180°+360°k.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: Use quadratic formula; only one root is valid in [−1,1].
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: Let u=sinx. Then u=[2 ± √(4+4)]/2 = 1 ± √2. u1=1+√2≈2.414 invalid. u2=1−√2≈−0.4142 valid. So sinx≈−0.4142. Reference angle r=sin⁻¹(0.4142)≈24.4°. Sine negative ⇒ QIII and QIV: x≈180°+24.4°=204.4° and x≈360°−24.4°=335.6°.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: Quadratic formula then solve sinx values.
Factorise if possible, else quadratic formula.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: 2sin^2x = 1 − sinx ⇒ 2u^2 + u − 1 = 0 (u=sinx). From Q51, u=1/2 or u=−1. Hence x=30°,150°,270°.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: cos(3x)=±1/2; list all x in range.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: 2−√3 = ( (√6−√2)/2 )^2, so sinx=±(√6−√2)/2. That corresponds to angles 15° and 165° for positive, and 195°,345° for negative. Hence x=15°,165°,195°,345°.
Replace sin^2x: (1−cos^2x)+cosx=1 ⇒ −cos^2x+cosx=0 ⇒ cosx(cosx−1)=0. So cosx=0 ⇒ x=90°,270°, or cosx=1 ⇒ x=0°,360°.
(1−sin^2x)+sinx=1 ⇒ −sin^2x+sinx=0 ⇒ sinx(sinx−1)=0. Thus sinx=0 ⇒ x=0°,180°,360°; or sinx=1 ⇒ x=90°.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Solve sin^2x + cos^2x + cosx = 1 for 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°.
Solve sin^2x + cos^2x + sinx = 0 for 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°.
Solve sin^2x + cos^2x = 0 for real x.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: sin^2x+cos^2x is always 1, never 0. Hence no real solution.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Solve sin^2x + sinx + 1 = 0 for real x.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: Let u=sinx. u^2+u+1 = (u+1/2)^2 + 3/4 > 0, so cannot be 0. Therefore no real solution.
u^2+2u+2=0 has Δ=4−8=−4<0 ⇒ no real u ⇒ no real x.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: u=sin(2x): u^2−2u+2=(u−1)^2+1>0, so cannot be 0. Hence no real solution.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: u^2−5u+6=(u−2)(u−3)=0 ⇒ u=2 or 3. Both are outside [−1,1], so cosx cannot take these values ⇒ no real solution.
u^2+5u+6=(u+2)(u+3)=0 ⇒ u=−2 or −3. Both impossible for sinx ⇒ no real solution.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Solve sin^2x + cos^2x + sinx + cosx = 0 for 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: Equation becomes 1 + (sinx+cosx)=0 ⇒ sinx+cosx=−1. Use sinx+cosx=√2 sin(x+45°). So √2 sin(x+45°)=−1 ⇒ sin(x+45°)=−1/√2 = −√2/2. Hence x+45°=225° or 315° (mod 360). So x=180° or 270° (within 0..360).

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Solve sin^2x + cos^2x + sinx − cosx = 0 for 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: Use identity then convert sinx−cosx to √2 sin(x−45°).

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: For real x, determine values of k such that sin^2x − k sinx + 1 = 0 has at least one solution.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: Need real u roots AND at least one root in [−1,1].
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: Let u=sinx. Need Δ=k^2−4≥0 ⇒ |k|≥2. Roots: u=(k±√(k^2−4))/2. For k≥2, the smaller root lies in (0,1] and is achievable, so solutions exist. For k≤−2, the larger root lies in [−1,0) and is also achievable, so solutions exist too. Hence solutions exist for |k|≥2.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Show that if |k|<2 then sin^2x − k sinx + 1 = 0 has no real solution.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: Let u=sinx. Quadratic u^2−ku+1=0 has real u only if Δ=k^2−4≥0. If |k|<2 then k^2−4<0, so there is no real u, hence no real sinx, hence no real x.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: Let t=tanx, factorise, then use tan period 180°.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: Let t = tanx. Then the equation becomes t^2 + 4t + 3 = 0. Factorise: (t+1)(t+3)=0, so t = −1 or t = −3. Case 1: tanx = −1. The reference angle is 45° because tan45°=1. Tangent is negative in Quadrants II and IV, so x = 180°−45° = 135° or x = 360°−45° = 315°. Case 2: tanx = −3. The reference angle is α = tan⁻¹(3) ≈ 71.565°. Again tangent negative ⇒ Quadrants II and IV: x = 180°−α ≈ 108.435° and x = 360°−α ≈ 288.435°. Therefore x ≈ 108.4°, 135.0°, 288.4°, 315.0° (to 1 d.p. where needed).

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Show that sin^2x + sinx + 2 = 0 has no real solution.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: Let u = sinx. Then u^2 + u + 2 = 0. For a quadratic au^2+bu+c=0 to have real solutions, Δ=b^2−4ac must be ≥0. Here a=1, b=1, c=2, so Δ = 1^2 − 4(1)(2) = 1 − 8 = −7 < 0. Hence u is not real. But sinx must be real for real x, so there is no real x satisfying sin^2x + sinx + 2 = 0.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: Rearrange to quadratic in sinx, factorise, reject invalid roots.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: Start with sin^2x = 2 − sinx. Bring all terms to one side: sin^2x + sinx − 2 = 0. Let u = sinx. Then u^2 + u − 2 = 0. Factorise: (u+2)(u−1)=0, so u=−2 or u=1. Since sinx ∈ [−1,1], u=−2 is impossible and must be rejected. Therefore sinx=1. On 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°, sinx=1 occurs at x=90°. So the only solution is x=90°.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: Let u=cos(2x), solve u(u−1)=0, then solve trig equations for x.
Let u=sin(2x), solve u(u−1)=0, then solve for x carefully.
Take square roots: sinx=±√2/2, then list angles.
Use cosx=±√2/2 and list within interval.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Show that sin^2x + 4 = 0 has no real solution.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: For all real x, sin^2x ≥ 0. Therefore sin^2x + 4 ≥ 4 > 0, so it cannot equal 0. Hence there is no real x satisfying sin^2x + 4 = 0.
cos^2x − 2cosx + 1 = (cosx−1)^2. So (cosx−1)^2=0 ⇒ cosx−1=0 ⇒ cosx=1. On 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°, cosx=1 at x=0° and x=360°. Therefore x=0°,360°.
sin^2x + 2sinx + 1 = (sinx+1)^2. So (sinx+1)^2=0 ⇒ sinx+1=0 ⇒ sinx=−1. On 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°, sinx=−1 at x=270°. Therefore x=270°.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: Factorise and reject any cos value outside [−1,1].
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: Let u=cosx. Then u^2 − 3u + 2 = 0. Factorise: (u−1)(u−2)=0 ⇒ u=1 or u=2. Since cosx cannot be 2, reject u=2. Therefore cosx=1 ⇒ x=0°,360°.
Let u=sinx. Then u^2 − 4u + 3 = 0 ⇒ (u−1)(u−3)=0 ⇒ u=1 or u=3. Since sinx cannot be 3, reject u=3. Therefore sinx=1 ⇒ x=90°.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: Convert to quadratic in sinx using cos^2x=1−sin^2x.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: Start: 2cos^2x = 1 + sinx. Substitute cos^2x = 1 − sin^2x: 2(1 − sin^2x)=1+sinx ⇒ 2 − 2sin^2x = 1 + sinx. Bring all terms to one side: 2sin^2x + sinx − 1 = 0. Let u=sinx. Solve: u = [−1 ± √(1+8)]/4 = [−1 ± 3]/4 ⇒ u=1/2 or u=−1. Now solve each: sinx=1/2 ⇒ x=30°,150°. sinx=−1 ⇒ x=270°. Therefore x=30°,150°,270°.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: Convert sin^2x to 1−cos^2x to form a quadratic in cosx.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: Start: 3sin^2x + 2cosx = 3. Replace sin^2x by 1−cos^2x: 3(1−cos^2x)+2cosx=3 ⇒ 3 − 3cos^2x + 2cosx = 3. Subtract 3 from both sides: −3cos^2x + 2cosx = 0. Factor: cosx(−3cosx+2)=0 ⇒ cosx=0 or cosx=2/3. If cosx=0 ⇒ x=90°,270°. If cosx=2/3 ⇒ x = cos⁻¹(2/3) ≈ 48.2°, and 360°−48.2° ≈ 311.8°. Therefore x≈48.2°, 90°, 270°, 311.8°.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: Convert sin^2x to 1−cos^2x to get quadratic in cosx.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: Start: 2sin^2x + cosx = 1. Substitute sin^2x = 1 − cos^2x: 2(1−cos^2x)+cosx=1 ⇒ 2 − 2cos^2x + cosx = 1. Rearranging: 2cos^2x − cosx − 1 = 0. Let u=cosx. Solve: u = [1 ± √(1+8)]/4 = [1 ± 3]/4 ⇒ u=1 or u=−1/2. If cosx=1 ⇒ x=0°,360°. If cosx=−1/2 ⇒ x=120°,240°. Therefore x=0°,120°,240°,360°.
Let u=sinx. Then u^2 + 2u = 0 ⇒ u(u+2)=0. So u=0 or u=−2. Since sinx cannot be −2, reject u=−2. Hence sinx=0 ⇒ x=0°,180°,360°.
Let u=cosx. Then u^2 + 2u = 0 ⇒ u(u+2)=0 ⇒ u=0 or u=−2. Reject u=−2. So cosx=0 ⇒ x=90°,270°.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Show that sin^2x = 1 − sinx can be written as sin^2x + sinx − 1 = 0.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: Move all terms to one side.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: Given sin^2x = 1 − sinx. Add sinx to both sides: sin^2x + sinx = 1. Subtract 1: sin^2x + sinx − 1 = 0.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Show that cos^2x + 3cosx + 3 = 0 has no real solution.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: Let u=cosx. Then u^2 + 3u + 3 = 0. Discriminant Δ = 3^2 − 4(1)(3) = 9 − 12 = −3 < 0. So u is not real, hence there is no real x satisfying the equation.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: tanx=±3; use principal angles and add 180°.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: tan^2x−9=0 ⇒ tan^2x=9 ⇒ tanx=±3. Let α=tan⁻¹(3)≈71.565°. For tanx=3 (Quadrants I and III): x≈α=71.6° and x≈α+180°=251.6°. For tanx=−3 (Quadrants II and IV): x≈180°−α=108.4° and x≈360°−α=288.4°. Hence x≈71.6°,108.4°,251.6°,288.4°.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Show that 1 − sin^2x − cosx = 0 becomes cos^2x − cosx = 0.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: Start with 1 − sin^2x − cosx = 0. Using the identity 1−sin^2x = cos^2x, substitute to get cos^2x − cosx = 0. (No further steps needed for equivalence.)

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Solve sin^2x − cos^2x = sinx − 1 for 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: Convert cos^2x to 1−sin^2x so equation becomes quadratic in sinx.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: Start with sin^2x − cos^2x = sinx − 1. Replace cos^2x by 1−sin^2x: sin^2x − (1−sin^2x) = sinx − 1 ⇒ sin^2x − 1 + sin^2x = sinx − 1 ⇒ 2sin^2x − 1 = sinx − 1. Add 1 to both sides: 2sin^2x = sinx. Bring to one side: 2sin^2x − sinx = 0 ⇒ sinx(2sinx−1)=0. So sinx=0 or sinx=1/2. If sinx=0 ⇒ x=0°,180°,360°. If sinx=1/2 ⇒ x=30°,150°. Therefore x=0°,30°,150°,180°,360°.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Solve sin^2x = sinx + 2 for real x.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: LHS: sin^2x ∈ [0,1]. RHS: sinx+2 ∈ [1,3]. For equality, RHS must lie in [0,1]. But RHS is always ≥1, and equals 1 only when sinx=−1. Check sinx=−1 gives LHS=1 and RHS=1, so it works. Therefore the only possibility is sinx=−1 ⇒ x=270°+360°k.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Show that sin^2x + 4sinx + 5 = 0 has no real solution.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: Let u=sinx. Then u^2 + 4u + 5 = 0. Discriminant Δ = 4^2 − 4·1·5 = 16 − 20 = −4 < 0. Hence u is not real, so there is no real x satisfying the equation.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: Let u=cos(2x); factorise; reject invalid root; solve remaining.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: Let u = cos(2x). Then u^2 − 4u + 3 = 0 ⇒ (u−1)(u−3)=0. So u=1 or u=3. Since cos(2x) cannot be 3, reject u=3. Therefore cos(2x)=1 ⇒ 2x = 0° + 360°k. For x in [0°,360°], 2x in [0°,720°], so 2x=0°,360°,720° ⇒ x=0°,180°,360°.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: Let u=sin(2x); factorise; reject sin(2x)=2; solve sin(2x)=1.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: Let u=sin(2x). Then u^2 − 3u + 2 = 0 ⇒ (u−1)(u−2)=0 ⇒ u=1 or u=2. Reject u=2 since sine cannot be 2. Thus sin(2x)=1 ⇒ 2x = 90° + 360°k. With 0°≤2x≤720°, we get 2x=90°,450° ⇒ x=45°,225°.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Show that sin^2x − k sinx + 1 = 0 has no real solution if |k|<2.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: Let u=sinx. The equation is u^2 − k u + 1 = 0. For real u, discriminant must satisfy Δ = k^2 − 4 ≥ 0. If |k|<2, then k^2<4 ⇒ k^2−4<0, so Δ<0 and there are no real roots u. Since sinx must be real, there is no real x. Hence no real solution when |k|<2.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Show that cos^2x − cosx + 1 > 0 for all real x.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: Let u=cosx and complete square or use Δ<0 with a>0.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: Let u=cosx (so u is real and in [−1,1]). Consider f(u)=u^2−u+1. Complete the square: u^2−u+1 = (u−1/2)^2 + 3/4. Since (u−1/2)^2 ≥ 0 for all real u, f(u) ≥ 3/4 > 0. Therefore cos^2x − cosx + 1 is strictly positive for all real x.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: tan(2x)=±1; solve 2x then divide by 2 carefully.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: Let t=tanx. Then t^2 + 2t + 5 = 0. Discriminant Δ = 2^2 − 4(1)(5) = 4 − 20 = −16 < 0. Thus there is no real t. Since tanx must be real for real x, there is no real x satisfying the equation.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: Rearrange to quadratic in cosx; reject invalid root; solve angles.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: Start with cos^2x = cosx + 1 ⇒ cos^2x − cosx − 1 = 0. Let u=cosx. Then u^2 − u − 1 = 0. Quadratic formula: u = [1 ± √(1 + 4)]/2 = (1 ± √5)/2. Now check range: (1+√5)/2 ≈ 1.618 > 1, invalid for cosine; reject it. Valid root is u = (1−√5)/2 ≈ −0.618. So cosx≈−0.618. Cosine negative in Quadrants II and III. Reference angle r = cos⁻¹(0.618) ≈ 51.8°. Therefore solutions are x ≈ 180°−51.8° = 128.2° and x ≈ 180°+51.8° = 231.8°.

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Express $\sin(90^\circ-x)+\cos x-2\sin x$ as a single trig function.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.hint: Use $\sin(90^\circ-x)=\cos x$, then combine $2\cos x-2\sin x=2\sqrt2\cos(x+45^\circ)$.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: $$\begin{aligned}\sin(90^\circ-x)+\cos x-2\sin x&=\cos x+\cos x-2\sin x\\&=2(\cos x-\sin x)\\&=2\big(\sqrt2\cos(x+45^\circ)\big)\\&=2\sqrt2\cos(x+45^\circ)\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Express $3\sin x-4\cos x$ in the form $R\sin(x-\alpha)$ with $R>0$.
Chapter 10-Trigonometric Identi.solution_text: $$\begin{aligned}3\sin x-4\cos x&=R\sin(x-\alpha)\\R&=\sqrt{3^2+(-4)^2}=5\\5\sin(x-\alpha)&=5(\sin x\cos\alpha-\cos x\sin\alpha)\\&=(5\cos\alpha)\sin x-(5\sin\alpha)\cos x\\5\cos\alpha&=3\Rightarrow \cos\alpha=\frac35\\5\sin\alpha&=4\Rightarrow \sin\alpha=\frac45\\\therefore\ 3\sin x-4\cos x&=5\sin(x-\alpha),\ \alpha\approx53.130^\circ\end{aligned}$$
